Al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel, and his time was between Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Most scholars hold that he was not a prophet. Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: he was a prophet.

If we say he was a slave, then his ethnicity is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib and Mujahid said: he was a Nubian, with split feet and thick lips. Al-Farra' and others said: he was an Abyssinian, with a flattened nose and thick lips.

It is also disputed what work he used to do. Khalid ibn al-Rabi' said: he was a carpenter. In the Ma'ani of al-Zajjaj it is said: he was a "najjad" (with a dal), [meaning a maker of cloaks or leather goods]. Ibn al-Musayyib said: he was a tailor. Ibn Abbas said: he was a shepherd. It was also said: he used to gather a bundle of firewood for his master every day.

This disagreement about whether he was free or a slave, about his ethnicity, and about what work he did, necessitates that none of these details be recorded or transmitted. However, the exegetes are fond of relating disputed reports as filler and for multiplication, whereas the correct course is to leave them aside.

The wisdom of Luqman is widely transmitted. Among it: it was said to him, "Who is the worst of people?" He said, "The one who does not mind that people see him doing evil." Dawud, peace be upon him, once said to him, "How have you woken up?" He said, "I have woken up in the hand of another." Dawud reflected on this and fainted [in a swoon]. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "I read more than ten thousand of the sayings of Luqman."

And "al-hikmah" (wisdom) is the speech through which one is admonished and alerted, and which people pass on to one another for that reason.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks): al-Zamakhshari said: "an" here is explanatory (mufassirah), because giving wisdom has the sense of saying. God, glorified is He, has alerted [us] that the original wisdom and true knowledge is acting upon them, or the worship of God and thanking Him, since he explained the giving of wisdom as inspiring [it] to gratitude. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom" so that he would thank God; thus he made it verbal-noun (masdariyyah, i.e., "that"), not explanatory. Sibawayh related: "I wrote to him with an-qum" (that stand up).

﴿Fa-innama yashkuru li-nafsihi﴾ (then he is grateful only for his own soul): that is, the reward of gratitude is attained only by those who are grateful, since He, exalted is He, is independent of gratitude. So the gratitude of the grateful does not benefit Him, and the ingratitude of the ungrateful does not harm Him. And ﴿Hamid﴾ (Praiseworthy) means deserving of praise in His essence and attributes.

﴿Wa-idh qala﴾ (And when he said): that is, "remember when." It was also said: it is possible that the implied meaning is: "And We gave him wisdom, when he said," and it was abbreviated because the preceding part indicates it. His son was dutiful. Other views: "or give thanks," "or be grateful," "or grateful" (he who is grateful).

﴿Wa-huwa ya'izuhu﴾ (while he was advising him) is a circumstantial clause (hal). It was said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he kept advising them until they both embraced Islam. The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong﴾, are from the speech of Luqman. It was also said: it is a report from God, separate from the speech of Luqman but connected to it for emphasis of meaning. In Sahih Muslim there is a report that apparently indicates it is from the speech of Luqman.

Al-Bazzi recited "Ya bunayya" with sukun (ya bunay), and "Ya bunayya innaha" with a kasrah on the ya, and "Ya bunayya aqim" with a fathah on it. It was also said: with sukun in the first and second, and kasrah in the middle. Hafs and al-Mufaddal from Asim recited with fathah in all three, on the reckoning of "Ya bunayya" with the fathah standing in for the alif (of address). The remaining seven [readers] recited with kasrah in all three.

﴿Wa-wassayna al-insana bi-walidayhi﴾ (And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents): when Luqman explained to his son that association is a wrong and forbade him from it, that was an incitement to obedience to God. Then [God] explained that obedience is due to the two parents, and explained the reason for it. So this is from the speech of Luqman, among what he enjoined upon his son, which God reported. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, said to Luqman; that is, "We said to him: be grateful," and "We said to him: and We have enjoined." It was also said: this verse is a clear interjection in the midst of Luqman's advice, and in it there is an emphasis and reinforcement for a child to follow his father and comply with his command in obedience to God, exalted is He.

Al-Qurtubi said: the correct view is that this verse and the verse of al-'Ankabut were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and a group of exegetes hold this view. Since [the verse] singled out the mother for the hardships of carrying, childbirth, nursing and raising, it drew attention to the cause that necessitates the enjoining. For this reason the hadith commands kindness to the mother three times, then mentions the father, giving him once a quarter of the kindness.

﴿Wahnan ala wahnin﴾ (weakness upon weakness): Ibn Abbas said: hardship after hardship, and creation after creation. Al-Dahhak said: weakness after weakness. Qatadah said: exertion upon exertion, meaning the weakness of pregnancy, the weakness of labour, and the weakness of postpartum bleeding. This word is in the accusative on these views as a circumstantial clause (hal). It was also said: ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾ refers to [the stages of] drop, then clot, until the end of the process of creation; on this view it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ḥamalat-hu (the object pronoun), which refers to the child.

Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu Amr, in one narration, recited "wahnan ala wahnin" with a fathah on the ha in both. This may be like "ash-sha'r" and "ash-sha'ar" (both forms of the word "hair"), or it may be the verbal noun of wahina (to be weak), yawhanu wahanan, with the fathah on the verbal noun as an analogical form. The majority recited with sukun on the ha in both. They also recited ﴿wa-fisaluhu﴾ (and his weaning). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub recited "wa-faslahu" (and his separation), and its meaning is weaning, that is, "in full two years," expressed by its endpoint. They agreed on counting two years for the period of nursing with regard to legal rulings and maintenance; as for the prohibition of relationship through nursing, there is a known difference of opinion in jurisprudence.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks) is in the accusative position according to al-Zajjaj's view. Al-Nahhas said: the better view is that it is explanatory (mufassirah). (To Me) means: for the blessing of faith.

﴿Wa-liwalidayka﴾ (and to your parents): for the blessing of upbringing. ﴿Ilayya al-masir﴾ (to Me is the final destination): a warning embedded within the advice.

﴿Wa-in jahadaka﴾ (But if they strive with you) up to ﴿fala tuti'huma﴾ (do not obey them): what was said about it has been discussed in al-'Ankabut, except that here it is ʿala (upon/to), while there it is li-tushrika (in order that you associate), with the particle of cause (lam al-'illah). ﴿Ma'ruf﴾ (kindness) is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "companionship," or "accompanying kindly," and good companionship; this consists of feeding and clothing them, not mistreating or scolding them, visiting them when they are ill, and burying them when they die.

﴿Wattabi' sabila man anaba ilayya﴾ (and follow the way of him who turns to Me): that is, who returns to God; and this is the way of the Messenger (ﷺ), not their way.

﴿Thumma ilayya marji'ukum﴾ (Then to Me is your return): that is, your return and their return, and I will requite each of you for his deeds.

When Luqman forbade his son from association, he alerted him to God's power and that nothing can be withheld from what He has power over. So he said: ﴿O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾ (yā bunayya innahā in taku mithqāla ḥabbatin). The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "innaha" (indeed it) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah, i.e., "indeed the matter"). Nafi' recited "mithqalu" with a ḍammah, reading "in taku" as complete (tāmmah, meaning "if it exists"). This is also the reading of al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far, and [the word] "mithqal" is reported with a masculine verb as if feminine because it is attached to a feminine noun; it is as if he said: "if it is the weight of a grain." The remaining seven recited with a fathah on mithqala, reading "in taku" as the incomplete (nāqiṣah) verb, whose subject is a pronoun understood from the context of the speech, estimated as "it," meaning the thing about which I asked.

It was reported that Luqman had asked his son: "Have you seen a grain that falls into the depths of the sea? Does God know it?" In this case the pronoun is a pronoun of a substance, not a pronoun of an accident, and this is supported by His words, ﴿if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Abd al-Karim al-Jazari recited "fa-takinna," with a kasrah on the kaf and the nun doubled, and also with a fathah. The reading of Muhammad ibn Abi Fajjah al-Ba'labakki was "fa-tukanna," with a ḍammah on the ta, a fathah on the kaf and the nun doubled. Qatadah recited "fa-takin," with a fathah on the ta, a kasrah on the kaf and sukun on the nun, from wakana yakinu (to be settled), and this reading is also reported from Abd al-Karim al-Jazari: that is, "it settles." The pronoun may be a pronoun of an accident, meaning that deed of obedience or disobedience. For the one who recites with the accusative of mithqal, the pronoun in "innaha" may be the pronoun of the deed, not the pronoun of the matter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads with the accusative, meaning "mithqal," the pronoun refers to the condition of wrongdoing or good-doing, that is, it was an example in smallness and insignificance, like the grain of mustard, and despite its smallness it was in the most hidden and most secure place, like the inside of a rock, or wherever it was, in the upper or lower world.

﴿Yati biha Allah﴾ (God will bring it forth): on the Day of Resurrection, and He will call it to account for it.

﴿Inna Allaha latif﴾ (Indeed God is Subtle): whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing.

﴿Khabir﴾ (Acquainted): knowing its essence. It is reported from Qatadah: Subtle in extracting it, Acquainted with its place of settlement. He began with what is related to it first, which is its being located (kaynunat al-shay').

﴿Fi sakhrah﴾ (within a rock): this is what is solid of the stone and difficult to extract from it. Then he followed it with the upper world, which is more strange to the hearer, then he followed it with what is the place of things for the observer, which is the earth. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi that this rock is the one upon which the earth rests. Ibn Abbas said: it is beneath the seven earths, in which the deeds of the wicked are recorded. Ibn Atiyyah said: it was said that he meant the rock upon which is the earth, the fish and the water, and it is upon the back of an angel. It was also said: it is a rock in the wind. All of this is weak, and its chain of transmission is not established; rather, the meaning of the speech is exaggeration and reaching the limit in conveying understanding, that is, His power reaches what is within the crevices of a rock, and what is in the heavens and the earth. End of quote.

It was said: the hiddenness of a thing is usually recognized by its smallness and by its distance from the observer, and by its being in darkness and being concealed. So "in a rock" is an indication of a veil, "in the heavens" an indication of distance, and "in the earth" an indication of darkness, for the interior of the earth is the darkest of places. In His words, ﴿God will bring it forth﴾, there is an indication of knowledge and power, as if He said: His knowledge and His power encompass it.

Having first forbidden him from associating partners with God, and then informed him of God's knowledge and His overwhelming power, He commanded him to do what brings him closer to God through acts of obedience. He began with the most noble of them, which is the prayer (al-salah), since in it one turns directly toward God. Then came enjoining good and forbidding evil, and then patience (sabr) in the face of all the trials that befall him, or in the face of what befalls him because of enjoining good upon those who would be moved by it and forbidding evil to those who reject it. The one who does this is often harmed. And this is only meant after he himself has become upright in his own soul and does what is good. ﴿Indeed that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before of what he was forbidden and commanded. Al-'azm (resolve, determination) is a verbal noun (masdar), so it may be taken in the sense of the passive participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolved upon," or in the sense of the active participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolute," as in His saying: ﴿Then when the matter is resolved upon﴾ [Muhammad: 21]. Ibn Juraij said: "of what God has resolved and commanded." It was also said: "of the noble characteristics and the resolute deeds of people of sound judgment, who travel the path of salvation." The apparent meaning is that it refers to the necessary obligations that follow from these matters, since the reference with "that" covers everything he was commanded and forbidden. The obedience (al-ta'at) mentioned here, the injunction of Luqman indicates, was commanded in all the religious communities (al-milal). Al-'azm means controlling the matter and attending to its proper rectification. Mu'arrij said: al-'azm means al-hazm (firmness), in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-hazm and al-'azm are both original roots, and what al-Mubarrad said, that the ʿayn was changed into a ḥāʾ, is not correct, because the inflections of each of the two words are consistently attested, so neither is the root of the other.

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾, that is: do not turn the side of your face to them as the arrogant person does, but face people with your countenance without pride or self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of scholars. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: He forbade him to humble himself without need. Ibn 'Atiyya gave something close to this as a possibility, saying: "It may also mean: nor [do you turn away from them in] asking or in begging out of poverty." He said: "The first interpretation, that of Ibn 'Abbas and the majority, is more apparent, because of the mention of strutting and vanity after it." Mujahid said: "﴿do not turn away﴾ means avoidance, like shunning someone by cursing his brother." Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "tusa''ir" (تُصَعِّرْ) with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the ʿayn. The rest of the seven read it with an alif (تُصاعِرْ). Al-Jahdari read "yusa''ir" (يُصَعِّرُ) as the imperfect of asʿara.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. The discussion of this clause has already been given in the surah of al-Isra' (Subhan).

﴿Indeed God does not love every arrogant boaster﴾. The discussion of a parallel of this clause was given in al-Nisa', in His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not love one who is self-deluded and boastful﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. When he (Luqman) enjoined his son to enjoin good and forbid evil, since he himself had become one who follows what is good and is restrained from what is evil, he commanded him to enjoin it on others and to forbid it to others. He forbade him from being haughty toward people, from self-admiration, and from walking exultantly. He informed him that God, exalted is He, does not love the mukhtal (the arrogant one), meaning the one who is proud, nor the fakhur (the boastful one). Mujahid said: "The fakhur is the one who enumerates what he has been given and does not thank God." The boasting (fakhr) by lineages also falls under the fakhur.

﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice﴾. When he forbade him from a blameworthy trait, he commanded him with a noble trait, which is moderation (al-qasd) in walking, such that one neither walks slowly, as those do who affect humility and those who feign admiration (for their own sake) do, dragging their steps slowly, the first for show and the second for pretended dignity, nor hastens as the reckless and rash person does. Abu Ja'far al-Mansur looked at Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and said: "All of you walk slowly, all of you seek prey, except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd." [p. 189] Ibn Mas'ud said: "They used to forbid the trot of the Jews and the crawl of the Christians, but (the proper way is) a walk between these two." It was also said that its meaning is: make your gaze fall at the place of your foot. It was read "wa-aqsid" (وأقْصِدْ) with a hamzat al-qat' (a cutting hamza, the hamza of the verb form of aqsada), meaning: aim straight in your walking, from aqsadahu al-rami, when the archer aims his arrow straight toward the target. Ibn Khalawayh attributed this reading to the Hijaz. Lowering the voice means reducing its loudness and its raising. Ghadd (lowering, restraining) means turning back the excessiveness of a thing, such as the voice, the gaze, or the reins. The Arabs used to boast of a loud voice and praise it in the pre-Islamic period, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Loud in speech, loud in sneezing, loud in appearance, loud in bounty;
and he strides on exhaustion with the stride of the ostrich, and he rises above men with a general (all-embracing) nature."

Lowering the voice is more beneficial for the speaker and more comforting to the listener's soul and understanding. In "a-nkar" (أَنْكَرَ), if it is formed from the passive verb, as in the saying: "a-shghal min dhat al-nihyayn" (more occupied than the one with two jars), its formation from this is anomalous (shadh). "Al-aswat" (the voices) means the voices of all animals. Some scholars said that "a-nkar" is for the blameworthy qualities attached to voices, and the donkey is a proverb for strong blame and insult. The raisers of their voices are compared to donkeys, and their voices to braying, without the particle of comparison, rather it is expressed as a metaphor (isti'ara), and this is the utmost exaggeration in blame and in repelling people from raising the voice. Since the voice of donkeys is uniform in itself and hardly differs in its harshness, it is given in the singular, because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar). As for the voices of donkeys, they are not very different, so it is pluralized in His saying: ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices﴾, meaning the most hateful of the voices of donkeys, with the plural without the definite article (lam). Al-Hasan said: The polytheists used to boast of raising their voices, so He answered them that if it were something good, donkeys would have been given superiority by it. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾ is from the words of Luqman to his son, as a warning against raising the voice, and the likeness of the donkey in this. It was said: it is from the words of God, exalted is He, and the counsel of Luqman ends at His saying: ﴿and lower your voice﴾, as a response from God against the polytheists who used to boast of loudness of voice. Raising the voice harms the listener and strikes the eardrum with force, and it may even tear the membrane that lies inside the ear. It was also said: ﴿and be moderate in your walking﴾ refers to actions, and ﴿and lower your voice﴾ refers to words, so He alerted to moderation in actions and to speaking little of superfluous words.

(p-186) ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom: "Be grateful to God. Whoever is grateful, is grateful only for his own soul. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy."﴾ ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him, "O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years: "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination."﴾ ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness, and follow the way of him who turns to Me in repentance. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿"O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed and is within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, God will bring it forth. Indeed, God is Subtle, Acquainted [with all things]."﴾ ﴿"O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination."﴾ ﴿"And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, God does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful."﴾ ﴿"And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys."﴾

It has been disputed about Luqman: was he free or a slave? If we say he was free, it is said that he was the son of Ba'ura. Wahb [ibn Munabbih] said: he was the son of the sister of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Muqatil said: he was the son of his maternal aunt. It was also said: he was of the offspring of Azar, lived one thousand years, met Dawud, peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him. He used to issue legal rulings (fatwa) before the mission of Dawud, and when Dawud was sent, he stopped issuing rulings. He was asked, "Why?" He said, "Am I not content when I have been relieved [of the burden]?" He was a judge among the Children of Israel. Al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel, and his time was between Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Most scholars hold that he was not a prophet. Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: he was a prophet.

If we say he was a slave, then his ethnicity is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib and Mujahid said: he was a Nubian, with split feet and thick lips. Al-Farra' and others said: he was an Abyssinian, with a flattened nose and thick lips.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub recited "wa-faslahu" (and his separation), and its meaning is weaning, that is, "in full two years," expressed by its endpoint. They agreed on counting two years for the period of nursing with regard to legal rulings and maintenance; as for the prohibition of relationship through nursing, there is a known difference of opinion in jurisprudence.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks) is in the accusative position according to al-Zajjaj's view. Al-Nahhas said: the better view is that it is explanatory (mufassirah). (To Me) means: for the blessing of faith.

﴿Wa-liwalidayka﴾ (and to your parents): for the blessing of upbringing. ﴿Ilayya al-masir﴾ (to Me is the final destination): a warning embedded within the advice.

﴿Wa-in jahadaka﴾ (But if they strive with you) up to ﴿fala tuti'huma﴾ (do not obey them): what was said about it has been discussed in al-'Ankabut, except that here it is ʿala (upon/to), while there it is li-tushrika (in order that you associate), with the particle of cause (lam al-'illah). ﴿Ma'ruf﴾ (kindness) is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "companionship," or "accompanying kindly," and good companionship; this consists of feeding and clothing them, not mistreating or scolding them, visiting them when they are ill, and burying them when they die.

﴿Wattabi' sabila man anaba ilayya﴾ (and follow the way of him who turns to Me): that is, who returns to God; and this is the way of the Messenger (ﷺ), not their way.

﴿Thumma ilayya marji'ukum﴾ (Then to Me is your return): that is, your return and their return, and I will requite each of you for his deeds.

When Luqman forbade his son from association, he alerted him to God's power and that nothing can be withheld from what He has power over. So he said: ﴿O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾ (yā bunayya innahā in taku mithqāla ḥabbatin). The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "innaha" (indeed it) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah, i.e., "indeed the matter"). Nafi' recited "mithqalu" with a ḍammah, reading "in taku" as complete (tāmmah, meaning "if it exists"). This is also the reading of al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far, and [the word] "mithqal" is reported with a masculine verb as if feminine because it is attached to a feminine noun; it is as if he said: "if it is the weight of a grain." The remaining seven recited with a fathah on mithqala, reading "in taku" as the incomplete (nāqiṣah) verb, whose subject is a pronoun understood from the context of the speech, estimated as "it," meaning the thing about which I asked.

It was reported that Luqman had asked his son: "Have you seen a grain that falls into the depths of the sea? Does God know it?" In this case the pronoun is a pronoun of a substance, not a pronoun of an accident, and this is supported by His words, ﴿if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Abd al-Karim al-Jazari recited "fa-takinna," with a kasrah on the kaf and the nun doubled, and also with a fathah. The reading of Muhammad ibn Abi Fajjah al-Ba'labakki was "fa-tukanna," with a ḍammah on the ta, a fathah on the kaf and the nun doubled. Qatadah recited "fa-takin," with a fathah on the ta, a kasrah on the kaf and sukun on the nun, from wakana yakinu (to be settled), and this reading is also reported from Abd al-Karim al-Jazari: that is, "it settles." The pronoun may be a pronoun of an accident, meaning that deed of obedience or disobedience. For the one who recites with the accusative of mithqal, the pronoun in "innaha" may be the pronoun of the deed, not the pronoun of the matter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads with the accusative, meaning "mithqal," the pronoun refers to the condition of wrongdoing or good-doing, that is, it was an example in smallness and insignificance, like the grain of mustard, and despite its smallness it was in the most hidden and most secure place, like the inside of a rock, or wherever it was, in the upper or lower world.

﴿Yati biha Allah﴾ (God will bring it forth): on the Day of Resurrection, and He will call it to account for it.

﴿Inna Allaha latif﴾ (Indeed God is Subtle): whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing.

﴿Khabir﴾ (Acquainted): knowing its essence. It is reported from Qatadah: Subtle in extracting it, Acquainted with its place of settlement. He began with what is related to it first, which is its being located (kaynunat al-shay').

﴿Fi sakhrah﴾ (within a rock): this is what is solid of the stone and difficult to extract from it. Then he followed it with the upper world, which is more strange to the hearer, then he followed it with what is the place of things for the observer, which is the earth. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi that this rock is the one upon which the earth rests. Ibn Abbas said: it is beneath the seven earths, in which the deeds of the wicked are recorded. Ibn Atiyyah said: it was said that he meant the rock upon which is the earth, the fish and the water, and it is upon the back of an angel. It was also said: it is a rock in the wind. All of this is weak, and its chain of transmission is not established; rather, the meaning of the speech is exaggeration and reaching the limit in conveying understanding, that is, His power reaches what is within the crevices of a rock, and what is in the heavens and the earth. End of quote.

It was said: the hiddenness of a thing is usually recognized by its smallness and by its distance from the observer, and by its being in darkness and being concealed. So "in a rock" is an indication of a veil, "in the heavens" an indication of distance, and "in the earth" an indication of darkness, for the interior of the earth is the darkest of places. In His words, ﴿God will bring it forth﴾, there is an indication of knowledge and power, as if He said: His knowledge and His power encompass it.

Having first forbidden him from associating partners with God, and then informed him of God's knowledge and His overwhelming power, He commanded him to do what brings him closer to God through acts of obedience. He began with the most noble of them, which is the prayer (al-salah), since in it one turns directly toward God. Then came enjoining good and forbidding evil, and then patience (sabr) in the face of all the trials that befall him, or in the face of what befalls him because of enjoining good upon those who would be moved by it and forbidding evil to those who reject it. The one who does this is often harmed. And this is only meant after he himself has become upright in his own soul and does what is good. ﴿Indeed that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before of what he was forbidden and commanded. Al-'azm (resolve, determination) is a verbal noun (masdar), so it may be taken in the sense of the passive participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolved upon," or in the sense of the active participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolute," as in His saying: ﴿Then when the matter is resolved upon﴾ [Muhammad: 21]. Ibn Juraij said: "of what God has resolved and commanded." It was also said: "of the noble characteristics and the resolute deeds of people of sound judgment, who travel the path of salvation." The apparent meaning is that it refers to the necessary obligations that follow from these matters, since the reference with "that" covers everything he was commanded and forbidden. The obedience (al-ta'at) mentioned here, the injunction of Luqman indicates, was commanded in all the religious communities (al-milal). Al-'azm means controlling the matter and attending to its proper rectification. Mu'arrij said: al-'azm means al-hazm (firmness), in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-hazm and al-'azm are both original roots, and what al-Mubarrad said, that the ʿayn was changed into a ḥāʾ, is not correct, because the inflections of each of the two words are consistently attested, so neither is the root of the other.

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾, that is: do not turn the side of your face to them as the arrogant person does, but face people with your countenance without pride or self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of scholars. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: He forbade him to humble himself without need. Ibn 'Atiyya gave something close to this as a possibility, saying: "It may also mean: nor [do you turn away from them in] asking or in begging out of poverty." He said: "The first interpretation, that of Ibn 'Abbas and the majority, is more apparent, because of the mention of strutting and vanity after it." Mujahid said: "﴿do not turn away﴾ means avoidance, like shunning someone by cursing his brother." Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "tusa''ir" (تُصَعِّرْ) with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the ʿayn. The rest of the seven read it with an alif (تُصاعِرْ). Al-Jahdari read "yusa''ir" (يُصَعِّرُ) as the imperfect of asʿara.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. The discussion of this clause has already been given in the surah of al-Isra' (Subhan).

﴿Indeed God does not love every arrogant boaster﴾. The discussion of a parallel of this clause was given in al-Nisa', in His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not love one who is self-deluded and boastful﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. When he (Luqman) enjoined his son to enjoin good and forbid evil, since he himself had become one who follows what is good and is restrained from what is evil, he commanded him to enjoin it on others and to forbid it to others. He forbade him from being haughty toward people, from self-admiration, and from walking exultantly. He informed him that God, exalted is He, does not love the mukhtal (the arrogant one), meaning the one who is proud, nor the fakhur (the boastful one). Mujahid said: "The fakhur is the one who enumerates what he has been given and does not thank God." The boasting (fakhr) by lineages also falls under the fakhur.

﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice﴾. When he forbade him from a blameworthy trait, he commanded him with a noble trait, which is moderation (al-qasd) in walking, such that one neither walks slowly, as those do who affect humility and those who feign admiration (for their own sake) do, dragging their steps slowly, the first for show and the second for pretended dignity, nor hastens as the reckless and rash person does. Abu Ja'far al-Mansur looked at Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and said: "All of you walk slowly, all of you seek prey, except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd." [p. 189] Ibn Mas'ud said: "They used to forbid the trot of the Jews and the crawl of the Christians, but (the proper way is) a walk between these two." It was also said that its meaning is: make your gaze fall at the place of your foot. It was read "wa-aqsid" (وأقْصِدْ) with a hamzat al-qat' (a cutting hamza, the hamza of the verb form of aqsada), meaning: aim straight in your walking, from aqsadahu al-rami, when the archer aims his arrow straight toward the target. Ibn Khalawayh attributed this reading to the Hijaz. Lowering the voice means reducing its loudness and its raising. Ghadd (lowering, restraining) means turning back the excessiveness of a thing, such as the voice, the gaze, or the reins. The Arabs used to boast of a loud voice and praise it in the pre-Islamic period, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Loud in speech, loud in sneezing, loud in appearance, loud in bounty;
and he strides on exhaustion with the stride of the ostrich, and he rises above men with a general (all-embracing) nature."

Lowering the voice is more beneficial for the speaker and more comforting to the listener's soul and understanding. In "a-nkar" (أَنْكَرَ), if it is formed from the passive verb, as in the saying: "a-shghal min dhat al-nihyayn" (more occupied than the one with two jars), its formation from this is anomalous (shadh). "Al-aswat" (the voices) means the voices of all animals. Some scholars said that "a-nkar" is for the blameworthy qualities attached to voices, and the donkey is a proverb for strong blame and insult. The raisers of their voices are compared to donkeys, and their voices to braying, without the particle of comparison, rather it is expressed as a metaphor (isti'ara), and this is the utmost exaggeration in blame and in repelling people from raising the voice. Since the voice of donkeys is uniform in itself and hardly differs in its harshness, it is given in the singular, because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar). As for the voices of donkeys, they are not very different, so it is pluralized in His saying: ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices﴾, meaning the most hateful of the voices of donkeys, with the plural without the definite article (lam). Al-Hasan said: The polytheists used to boast of raising their voices, so He answered them that if it were something good, donkeys would have been given superiority by it. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾ is from the words of Luqman to his son, as a warning against raising the voice, and the likeness of the donkey in this. It was said: it is from the words of God, exalted is He, and the counsel of Luqman ends at His saying: ﴿and lower your voice﴾, as a response from God against the polytheists who used to boast of loudness of voice. Raising the voice harms the listener and strikes the eardrum with force, and it may even tear the membrane that lies inside the ear. It was also said: ﴿and be moderate in your walking﴾ refers to actions, and ﴿and lower your voice﴾ refers to words, so He alerted to moderation in actions and to speaking little of superfluous words.

(p-186) ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom: "Be grateful to God. Whoever is grateful, is grateful only for his own soul. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy."﴾ ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him, "O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years: "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination."﴾ ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness, and follow the way of him who turns to Me in repentance. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿"O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed and is within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, God will bring it forth. Indeed, God is Subtle, Acquainted [with all things]."﴾ ﴿"O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination."﴾ ﴿"And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, God does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful."﴾ ﴿"And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys."﴾

It has been disputed about Luqman: was he free or a slave? If we say he was free, it is said that he was the son of Ba'ura. Wahb [ibn Munabbih] said: he was the son of the sister of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Muqatil said: he was the son of his maternal aunt. It was also said: he was of the offspring of Azar, lived one thousand years, met Dawud, peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him. He used to issue legal rulings (fatwa) before the mission of Dawud, and when Dawud was sent, he stopped issuing rulings. He was asked, "Why?" He said, "Am I not content when I have been relieved [of the burden]?" He was a judge among the Children of Israel. Al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel, and his time was between Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Most scholars hold that he was not a prophet. Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: he was a prophet.

If we say he was a slave, then his ethnicity is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib and Mujahid said: he was a Nubian, with split feet and thick lips. Al-Farra' and others said: he was an Abyssinian, with a flattened nose and thick lips.

It is also disputed what work he used to do. Khalid ibn al-Rabi' said: he was a carpenter. In the Ma'ani of al-Zajjaj it is said: he was a "najjad" (with a dal), [meaning a maker of cloaks or leather goods]. Ibn al-Musayyib said: he was a tailor. Ibn Abbas said: he was a shepherd. It was also said: he used to gather a bundle of firewood for his master every day.

This disagreement about whether he was free or a slave, about his ethnicity, and about what work he did, necessitates that none of these details be recorded or transmitted. However, the exegetes are fond of relating disputed reports as filler and for multiplication, whereas the correct course is to leave them aside.

The wisdom of Luqman is widely transmitted. Among it: it was said to him, "Who is the worst of people?" He said, "The one who does not mind that people see him doing evil." Dawud, peace be upon him, once said to him, "How have you woken up?" He said, "I have woken up in the hand of another." Dawud reflected on this and fainted [in a swoon]. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "I read more than ten thousand of the sayings of Luqman."

And "al-hikmah" (wisdom) is the speech through which one is admonished and alerted, and which people pass on to one another for that reason.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks): al-Zamakhshari said: "an" here is explanatory (mufassirah), because giving wisdom has the sense of saying. God, glorified is He, has alerted [us] that the original wisdom and true knowledge is acting upon them, or the worship of God and thanking Him, since he explained the giving of wisdom as inspiring [it] to gratitude. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom" so that he would thank God; thus he made it verbal-noun (masdariyyah, i.e., "that"), not explanatory. Sibawayh related: "I wrote to him with an-qum" (that stand up).

﴿Fa-innama yashkuru li-nafsihi﴾ (then he is grateful only for his own soul): that is, the reward of gratitude is attained only by those who are grateful, since He, exalted is He, is independent of gratitude. So the gratitude of the grateful does not benefit Him, and the ingratitude of the ungrateful does not harm Him. And ﴿Hamid﴾ (Praiseworthy) means deserving of praise in His essence and attributes.

﴿Wa-idh qala﴾ (And when he said): that is, "remember when." It was also said: it is possible that the implied meaning is: "And We gave him wisdom, when he said," and it was abbreviated because the preceding part indicates it. His son was dutiful. Other views: "or give thanks," "or be grateful," "or grateful" (he who is grateful).

﴿Wa-huwa ya'izuhu﴾ (while he was advising him) is a circumstantial clause (hal). It was said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he kept advising them until they both embraced Islam. The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong﴾, are from the speech of Luqman. It was also said: it is a report from God, separate from the speech of Luqman but connected to it for emphasis of meaning. In Sahih Muslim there is a report that apparently indicates it is from the speech of Luqman.

Al-Bazzi recited "Ya bunayya" with sukun (ya bunay), and "Ya bunayya innaha" with a kasrah on the ya, and "Ya bunayya aqim" with a fathah on it. It was also said: with sukun in the first and second, and kasrah in the middle. Hafs and al-Mufaddal from Asim recited with fathah in all three, on the reckoning of "Ya bunayya" with the fathah standing in for the alif (of address). The remaining seven [readers] recited with kasrah in all three.

﴿Wa-wassayna al-insana bi-walidayhi﴾ (And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents): when Luqman explained to his son that association is a wrong and forbade him from it, that was an incitement to obedience to God. Then [God] explained that obedience is due to the two parents, and explained the reason for it. So this is from the speech of Luqman, among what he enjoined upon his son, which God reported. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, said to Luqman; that is, "We said to him: be grateful," and "We said to him: and We have enjoined." It was also said: this verse is a clear interjection in the midst of Luqman's advice, and in it there is an emphasis and reinforcement for a child to follow his father and comply with his command in obedience to God, exalted is He.

Al-Qurtubi said: the correct view is that this verse and the verse of al-'Ankabut were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and a group of exegetes hold this view. Since [the verse] singled out the mother for the hardships of carrying, childbirth, nursing and raising, it drew attention to the cause that necessitates the enjoining. For this reason the hadith commands kindness to the mother three times, then mentions the father, giving him once a quarter of the kindness.

﴿Wahnan ala wahnin﴾ (weakness upon weakness): Ibn Abbas said: hardship after hardship, and creation after creation. Al-Dahhak said: weakness after weakness. Qatadah said: exertion upon exertion, meaning the weakness of pregnancy, the weakness of labour, and the weakness of postpartum bleeding. This word is in the accusative on these views as a circumstantial clause (hal). It was also said: ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾ refers to [the stages of] drop, then clot, until the end of the process of creation; on this view it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ḥamalat-hu (the object pronoun), which refers to the child.

Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu Amr, in one narration, recited "wahnan ala wahnin" with a fathah on the ha in both. This may be like "ash-sha'r" and "ash-sha'ar" (both forms of the word "hair"), or it may be the verbal noun of wahina (to be weak), yawhanu wahanan, with the fathah on the verbal noun as an analogical form. Having first forbidden him from associating partners with God, and then informed him of God's knowledge and His overwhelming power, He commanded him to do what brings him closer to God through acts of obedience. He began with the most noble of them, which is the prayer (al-salah), since in it one turns directly toward God. Then came enjoining good and forbidding evil, and then patience (sabr) in the face of all the trials that befall him, or in the face of what befalls him because of enjoining good upon those who would be moved by it and forbidding evil to those who reject it. The one who does this is often harmed. And this is only meant after he himself has become upright in his own soul and does what is good. ﴿Indeed that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before of what he was forbidden and commanded. Al-'azm (resolve, determination) is a verbal noun (masdar), so it may be taken in the sense of the passive participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolved upon," or in the sense of the active participle, meaning "of the matters that are resolute," as in His saying: ﴿Then when the matter is resolved upon﴾ [Muhammad: 21]. Ibn Juraij said: "of what God has resolved and commanded." It was also said: "of the noble characteristics and the resolute deeds of people of sound judgment, who travel the path of salvation." The apparent meaning is that it refers to the necessary obligations that follow from these matters, since the reference with "that" covers everything he was commanded and forbidden. The obedience (al-ta'at) mentioned here, the injunction of Luqman indicates, was commanded in all the religious communities (al-milal). Al-'azm means controlling the matter and attending to its proper rectification. Mu'arrij said: al-'azm means al-hazm (firmness), in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-hazm and al-'azm are both original roots, and what al-Mubarrad said, that the ʿayn was changed into a ḥāʾ, is not correct, because the inflections of each of the two words are consistently attested, so neither is the root of the other.

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾, that is: do not turn the side of your face to them as the arrogant person does, but face people with your countenance without pride or self-admiration. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of scholars. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: He forbade him to humble himself without need. Ibn 'Atiyya gave something close to this as a possibility, saying: "It may also mean: nor [do you turn away from them in] asking or in begging out of poverty." He said: "The first interpretation, that of Ibn 'Abbas and the majority, is more apparent, because of the mention of strutting and vanity after it." Mujahid said: "﴿do not turn away﴾ means avoidance, like shunning someone by cursing his brother." Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "tusa''ir" (تُصَعِّرْ) with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a shaddah on the ʿayn. The rest of the seven read it with an alif (تُصاعِرْ). Al-Jahdari read "yusa''ir" (يُصَعِّرُ) as the imperfect of asʿara.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. The discussion of this clause has already been given in the surah of al-Isra' (Subhan).

﴿Indeed God does not love every arrogant boaster﴾. The discussion of a parallel of this clause was given in al-Nisa', in His saying: ﴿Indeed God does not love one who is self-deluded and boastful﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. When he (Luqman) enjoined his son to enjoin good and forbid evil, since he himself had become one who follows what is good and is restrained from what is evil, he commanded him to enjoin it on others and to forbid it to others. He forbade him from being haughty toward people, from self-admiration, and from walking exultantly. He informed him that God, exalted is He, does not love the mukhtal (the arrogant one), meaning the one who is proud, nor the fakhur (the boastful one). Mujahid said: "The fakhur is the one who enumerates what he has been given and does not thank God." The boasting (fakhr) by lineages also falls under the fakhur.

﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice﴾. When he forbade him from a blameworthy trait, he commanded him with a noble trait, which is moderation (al-qasd) in walking, such that one neither walks slowly, as those do who affect humility and those who feign admiration (for their own sake) do, dragging their steps slowly, the first for show and the second for pretended dignity, nor hastens as the reckless and rash person does. Abu Ja'far al-Mansur looked at Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and said: "All of you walk slowly, all of you seek prey, except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd." [p. 189] Ibn Mas'ud said: "They used to forbid the trot of the Jews and the crawl of the Christians, but (the proper way is) a walk between these two." It was also said that its meaning is: make your gaze fall at the place of your foot. It was read "wa-aqsid" (وأقْصِدْ) with a hamzat al-qat' (a cutting hamza, the hamza of the verb form of aqsada), meaning: aim straight in your walking, from aqsadahu al-rami, when the archer aims his arrow straight toward the target. Ibn Khalawayh attributed this reading to the Hijaz. Lowering the voice means reducing its loudness and its raising. Ghadd (lowering, restraining) means turning back the excessiveness of a thing, such as the voice, the gaze, or the reins. The Arabs used to boast of a loud voice and praise it in the pre-Islamic period, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Loud in speech, loud in sneezing, loud in appearance, loud in bounty;
and he strides on exhaustion with the stride of the ostrich, and he rises above men with a general (all-embracing) nature."

Lowering the voice is more beneficial for the speaker and more comforting to the listener's soul and understanding. In "a-nkar" (أَنْكَرَ), if it is formed from the passive verb, as in the saying: "a-shghal min dhat al-nihyayn" (more occupied than the one with two jars), its formation from this is anomalous (shadh). "Al-aswat" (the voices) means the voices of all animals. Some scholars said that "a-nkar" is for the blameworthy qualities attached to voices, and the donkey is a proverb for strong blame and insult. The raisers of their voices are compared to donkeys, and their voices to braying, without the particle of comparison, rather it is expressed as a metaphor (isti'ara), and this is the utmost exaggeration in blame and in repelling people from raising the voice. Since the voice of donkeys is uniform in itself and hardly differs in its harshness, it is given in the singular, because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar). As for the voices of donkeys, they are not very different, so it is pluralized in His saying: ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices﴾, meaning the most hateful of the voices of donkeys, with the plural without the definite article (lam). Al-Hasan said: The polytheists used to boast of raising their voices, so He answered them that if it were something good, donkeys would have been given superiority by it. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Indeed the most hateful of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾ is from the words of Luqman to his son, as a warning against raising the voice, and the likeness of the donkey in this. It was said: it is from the words of God, exalted is He, and the counsel of Luqman ends at His saying: ﴿and lower your voice﴾, as a response from God against the polytheists who used to boast of loudness of voice. Raising the voice harms the listener and strikes the eardrum with force, and it may even tear the membrane that lies inside the ear. It was also said: ﴿and be moderate in your walking﴾ refers to actions, and ﴿and lower your voice﴾ refers to words, so He alerted to moderation in actions and to speaking little of superfluous words.

(p-186) ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom: "Be grateful to God. Whoever is grateful, is grateful only for his own soul. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy."﴾ ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him, "O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years: "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination."﴾ ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness, and follow the way of him who turns to Me in repentance. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿"O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed and is within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, God will bring it forth. Indeed, God is Subtle, Acquainted [with all things]."﴾ ﴿"O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination."﴾ ﴿"And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, God does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful."﴾ ﴿"And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys."﴾

It has been disputed about Luqman: was he free or a slave? If we say he was free, it is said that he was the son of Ba'ura. Wahb [ibn Munabbih] said: he was the son of the sister of Ayyub, peace be upon him. Muqatil said: he was the son of his maternal aunt. It was also said: he was of the offspring of Azar, lived one thousand years, met Dawud, peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him. He used to issue legal rulings (fatwa) before the mission of Dawud, and when Dawud was sent, he stopped issuing rulings. He was asked, "Why?" He said, "Am I not content when I have been relieved [of the burden]?" He was a judge among the Children of Israel. Al-Waqidi said: he was a judge among the Children of Israel, and his time was between Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Most scholars hold that he was not a prophet. Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: he was a prophet.

If we say he was a slave, then his ethnicity is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyib and Mujahid said: he was a Nubian, with split feet and thick lips. Al-Farra' and others said: he was an Abyssinian, with a flattened nose and thick lips.

It is also disputed what work he used to do. Khalid ibn al-Rabi' said: he was a carpenter. In the Ma'ani of al-Zajjaj it is said: he was a "najjad" (with a dal), [meaning a maker of cloaks or leather goods]. Ibn al-Musayyib said: he was a tailor. Ibn Abbas said: he was a shepherd. It was also said: he used to gather a bundle of firewood for his master every day.

This disagreement about whether he was free or a slave, about his ethnicity, and about what work he did, necessitates that none of these details be recorded or transmitted. However, the exegetes are fond of relating disputed reports as filler and for multiplication, whereas the correct course is to leave them aside.

The wisdom of Luqman is widely transmitted. Among it: it was said to him, "Who is the worst of people?" He said, "The one who does not mind that people see him doing evil." Dawud, peace be upon him, once said to him, "How have you woken up?" He said, "I have woken up in the hand of another." Dawud reflected on this and fainted [in a swoon]. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "I read more than ten thousand of the sayings of Luqman."

And "al-hikmah" (wisdom) is the speech through which one is admonished and alerted, and which people pass on to one another for that reason.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks): al-Zamakhshari said: "an" here is explanatory (mufassirah), because giving wisdom has the sense of saying. God, glorified is He, has alerted [us] that the original wisdom and true knowledge is acting upon them, or the worship of God and thanking Him, since he explained the giving of wisdom as inspiring [it] to gratitude. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom" so that he would thank God; thus he made it verbal-noun (masdariyyah, i.e., "that"), not explanatory. Sibawayh related: "I wrote to him with an-qum" (that stand up).

﴿Fa-innama yashkuru li-nafsihi﴾ (then he is grateful only for his own soul): that is, the reward of gratitude is attained only by those who are grateful, since He, exalted is He, is independent of gratitude. So the gratitude of the grateful does not benefit Him, and the ingratitude of the ungrateful does not harm Him. And ﴿Hamid﴾ (Praiseworthy) means deserving of praise in His essence and attributes.

﴿Wa-idh qala﴾ (And when he said): that is, "remember when." It was also said: it is possible that the implied meaning is: "And We gave him wisdom, when he said," and it was abbreviated because the preceding part indicates it. His son was dutiful. Other views: "or give thanks," "or be grateful," "or grateful" (he who is grateful).

﴿Wa-huwa ya'izuhu﴾ (while he was advising him) is a circumstantial clause (hal). It was said: his son and his wife were disbelievers, and he kept advising them until they both embraced Islam. The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿Indeed, association [of partners with God] is a great wrong﴾, are from the speech of Luqman. It was also said: it is a report from God, separate from the speech of Luqman but connected to it for emphasis of meaning. In Sahih Muslim there is a report that apparently indicates it is from the speech of Luqman.

Al-Bazzi recited "Ya bunayya" with sukun (ya bunay), and "Ya bunayya innaha" with a kasrah on the ya, and "Ya bunayya aqim" with a fathah on it. It was also said: with sukun in the first and second, and kasrah in the middle. Hafs and al-Mufaddal from Asim recited with fathah in all three, on the reckoning of "Ya bunayya" with the fathah standing in for the alif (of address). The remaining seven [readers] recited with kasrah in all three.

﴿Wa-wassayna al-insana bi-walidayhi﴾ (And We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents): when Luqman explained to his son that association is a wrong and forbade him from it, that was an incitement to obedience to God. Then [God] explained that obedience is due to the two parents, and explained the reason for it. So this is from the speech of Luqman, among what he enjoined upon his son, which God reported. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, said to Luqman; that is, "We said to him: be grateful," and "We said to him: and We have enjoined." It was also said: this verse is a clear interjection in the midst of Luqman's advice, and in it there is an emphasis and reinforcement for a child to follow his father and comply with his command in obedience to God, exalted is He.

Al-Qurtubi said: the correct view is that this verse and the verse of al-'Ankabut were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and a group of exegetes hold this view. Since [the verse] singled out the mother for the hardships of carrying, childbirth, nursing and raising, it drew attention to the cause that necessitates the enjoining. For this reason the hadith commands kindness to the mother three times, then mentions the father, giving him once a quarter of the kindness.

﴿Wahnan ala wahnin﴾ (weakness upon weakness): Ibn Abbas said: hardship after hardship, and creation after creation. Al-Dahhak said: weakness after weakness. Qatadah said: exertion upon exertion, meaning the weakness of pregnancy, the weakness of labour, and the weakness of postpartum bleeding. This word is in the accusative on these views as a circumstantial clause (hal). It was also said: ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾ refers to [the stages of] drop, then clot, until the end of the process of creation; on this view it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ḥamalat-hu (the object pronoun), which refers to the child.

Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu Amr, in one narration, recited "wahnan ala wahnin" with a fathah on the ha in both. This may be like "ash-sha'r" and "ash-sha'ar" (both forms of the word "hair"), or it may be the verbal noun of wahina (to be weak), yawhanu wahanan, with the fathah on the verbal noun as an analogical form. The majority recited with sukun on the ha in both. They also recited ﴿wa-fisaluhu﴾ (and his weaning). Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub recited "wa-faslahu" (and his separation), and its meaning is weaning, that is, "in full two years," expressed by its endpoint. They agreed on counting two years for the period of nursing with regard to legal rulings and maintenance; as for the prohibition of relationship through nursing, there is a known difference of opinion in jurisprudence.

﴿An-ishkur﴾ (that give thanks) is in the accusative position according to al-Zajjaj's view. Al-Nahhas said: the better view is that it is explanatory (mufassirah). (To Me) means: for the blessing of faith.

﴿Wa-liwalidayka﴾ (and to your parents): for the blessing of upbringing. ﴿Ilayya al-masir﴾ (to Me is the final destination): a warning embedded within the advice.

﴿Wa-in jahadaka﴾ (But if they strive with you) up to ﴿fala tuti'huma﴾ (do not obey them): what was said about it has been discussed in al-'Ankabut, except that here it is ʿala (upon/to), while there it is li-tushrika (in order that you associate), with the particle of cause (lam al-'illah). ﴿Ma'ruf﴾ (kindness) is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "companionship," or "accompanying kindly," and good companionship; this consists of feeding and clothing them, not mistreating or scolding them, visiting them when they are ill, and burying them when they die.

﴿Wattabi' sabila man anaba ilayya﴾ (and follow the way of him who turns to Me): that is, who returns to God; and this is the way of the Messenger (ﷺ), not their way.

﴿Thumma ilayya marji'ukum﴾ (Then to Me is your return): that is, your return and their return, and I will requite each of you for his deeds.

When Luqman forbade his son from association, he alerted him to God's power and that nothing can be withheld from what He has power over. So he said: ﴿O my son, indeed if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾ (yā bunayya innahā in taku mithqāla ḥabbatin). The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "innaha" (indeed it) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah, i.e., "indeed the matter"). Nafi' recited "mithqalu" with a ḍammah, reading "in taku" as complete (tāmmah, meaning "if it exists"). This is also the reading of al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far, and [the word] "mithqal" is reported with a masculine verb as if feminine because it is attached to a feminine noun; it is as if he said: "if it is the weight of a grain." The remaining seven recited with a fathah on mithqala, reading "in taku" as the incomplete (nāqiṣah) verb, whose subject is a pronoun understood from the context of the speech, estimated as "it," meaning the thing about which I asked.

It was reported that Luqman had asked his son: "Have you seen a grain that falls into the depths of the sea? Does God know it?" In this case the pronoun is a pronoun of a substance, not a pronoun of an accident, and this is supported by His words, ﴿if it is [even] the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Abd al-Karim al-Jazari recited "fa-takinna," with a kasrah on the kaf and the nun doubled, and also with a fathah. The reading of Muhammad ibn Abi Fajjah al-Ba'labakki was "fa-tukanna," with a ḍammah on the ta, a fathah on the kaf and the nun doubled. Qatadah recited "fa-takin," with a fathah on the ta, a kasrah on the kaf and sukun on the nun, from wakana yakinu (to be settled), and this reading is also reported from Abd al-Karim al-Jazari: that is, "it settles." The pronoun may be a pronoun of an accident, meaning that deed of obedience or disobedience. For the one who recites with the accusative of mithqal, the pronoun in "innaha" may be the pronoun of the deed, not the pronoun of the matter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: whoever reads with the accusative, meaning "mithqal," the pronoun refers to the condition of wrongdoing or good-doing, that is, it was an example in smallness and insignificance, like the grain of mustard, and despite its smallness it was in the most hidden and most secure place, like the inside of a rock, or wherever it was, in the upper or lower world.

﴿Yati biha Allah﴾ (God will bring it forth): on the Day of Resurrection, and He will call it to account for it.

﴿Inna Allaha latif﴾ (Indeed God is Subtle): whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing.

﴿Khabir﴾ (Acquainted): knowing its essence. It is reported from Qatadah: Subtle in extracting it, Acquainted with its place of settlement. He began with what is related to it first, which is its being located (kaynunat al-shay').

﴿Fi sakhrah﴾ (within a rock): this is what is solid of the stone and difficult to extract from it. Then he followed it with the upper world, which is more strange to the hearer, then he followed it with what is the place of things for the observer, which is the earth. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi that this rock is the one upon which the earth rests. Ibn Abbas said: it is beneath the seven earths, in which the deeds of the wicked are recorded. Ibn Atiyyah said: it was said that he meant the rock upon which is the earth, the fish and the water, and it is upon the back of an angel. It was also said: it is a rock in the wind. All of this is weak, and its chain of transmission is not established; rather, the meaning of the speech is exaggeration and reaching the limit in conveying understanding, that is, His power reaches what is within the crevices of a rock, and what is in the heavens and the earth. End of quote.

It was said: the hiddenness of a thing is usually recognized by its smallness and by its distance from the observer, and by its being in darkness and being concealed. So "in a rock" is an indication of a veil, "in the heavens" an indication of distance, and "in the earth" an indication of darkness, for the interior of the earth is the darkest of places. In His words, ﴿God will bring it forth﴾, there is an indication of knowledge and power, as if He said: His knowledge and His power encompass it.
