**(p-193)** ﴿Do you not see that Allah causes the night to merge into the day and causes the day to merge into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term, and that Allah is Aware of what you do?﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Great.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that the ships sail upon the sea by the favour of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is steadfast and grateful.﴾ ﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate.﴾ ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail his son at all, nor will a son avail his father at all. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, so let not the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.﴾

﴿يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ﴾: I have explained these two clauses in Surat Al 'Imran and here.

﴿إلى أجَلٍ﴾: The preposition ilā (to) indicates the endpoint, meaning that it reaches it and terminates at it. In Surat az-Zumar the phrase is ﴿لِأجَلٍ﴾ [az-Zumar: 5], which indicates exclusivity, by making the running specifically aimed at attaining a specified term. The running of the sun is specific to the end of the year, and the running of the moon to the end of the month. Both meanings suit their running, which is why the verb takes these two prepositions. ʿAyyāsh, on the authority of Abū ʿAmr, read ﴿بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ with the yā of the third person (ghayba).

﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ (the verse): its explanation has been given in Surat al-Hajj and here.

﴿وأنَّ ما يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ الباطِلُ﴾: In al-Hajj it is ﴿مِن دُونِهِ هو الباطِلُ﴾ [al-Hajj: 62], with the addition of "huwa." When the Exalted mentioned the subjugation of the two luminaries and His favour upon us through it, He also mentioned who subjected the ships from the earthly world, by the common factor they share, which is motion. The majority read ﴿بِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ in the singular form (ifrād lafẓī). Al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Yaʿmar read ﴿بِنِعْماتِ اللَّهِ﴾ with a kasra on the nūn and sukūn on the ʿayn, in the plural with alif and tā'. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with a fatḥa on the nūn and kasra on the ʿayn, with alif, tā' and the bā'. The bā' may be causal (sababiyya), meaning that it runs because of the wind and Allah's subjugation, or circumstantial (ḥāliyya, a ḥāl clause), meaning accompanied by Allah's favour, which is what the ships carry of food, provisions and merchandise. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the bā' is for adhesion (ilṣāq). End of quote. Mūsā ibn az-Zubayr read ﴿الفُلُكَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the lām. ﴿صَبّارٍ شَكُورٍ﴾ are two intensive patterns (ṣīghat mubālagha), and fa‘‘āl is more emphatic because of the increase in its letters.

Since the running of the ship on the sea was mentioned, and there is in that what the rider cannot fail to feel of fear, and since the favour was mentioned, it fits to conclude with patience toward what is feared and gratitude for what Allah has bestowed. He likened the wave, in its height, its blackness and its turbulence, to the ẓulal, which is the clouds. It was also said that ka-ẓ-ẓulal means like mountains, since a mountain is also called ẓulla. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya read ﴿كالظِّلالِ﴾, and both are plurals of ẓulla, like qulla, qulal and qilal. His saying ﴿وإذا غَشِيَهُمْ﴾ contains an iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person), moving from the second-person pronoun in ﴿لِيُرِيَكُمْ﴾ to the third-person pronoun in ﴿غَشِيَهُمْ﴾. ﴿مَوْجٌ﴾ is a collective noun (ism jins) distinguished from its singular by the feminine tā', so it indicates plurality, and that is why it was likened to a plural.

﴿فَمِنهم مُقْتَصِدٌ﴾: al-Ḥasan said: i.e. a believer who recognises Allah's right in these blessings. Mujāhid said: moderate in his disbelief, i.e. he submits to Allah and understands that such power is from Him, even though he goes astray in the idols in that he exalts them. It was also said: or moderate in the sincerity he had at sea. az-Zamakhsharī said: meaning that this sincerity arising at the time of fear is not befitting for anyone ever. End of quote. az-Zamakhsharī frequently used qaṭṭ as an adverb, while its governing element is not a past-tense verb, which contradicts Arabic usage in this matter. Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is steadfast and grateful.﴾ ﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. None denies Our signs except every treacherous ingrate.﴾ ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail his son at all, nor will a son avail his father at all. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, so let not the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Deceiver deceive you about Allah.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware.﴾
